exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the snow, the light, and the silence do the talking. Shepitko shoots betrayal and faith with the same stark patience.

name: Elem Klimov
teaser: Soviet director of Come and See, one of the most harrowing war films ever made. He made few films; he meant the ones he made to stay with you.

exploreAction.targetName: Come and See (1985) — the first 20 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Notice how the film lets you feel the village's warmth before the war arrives. That warmth makes everything after unbearable.

name: Béla Tarr
teaser: Hungarian master of the long take who declared he only makes films about the fall of humanity and the absurdity of its existence. His shots can last ten minutes.

exploreAction.targetName: Werckmeister Harmonies (2000) — the hospital corridor scene
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the whole sequence in one sitting. The camera never cuts; your attention becomes part of the film's machinery.

name: Miklós Jancsó
teaser: Hungarian director who turned the tracking shot into a political instrument — his cavalry and dance sequences are choreographed like battle ballets.

exploreAction.instruction: Count how many times the camera moves in a full circle. Jancsó maps power, betrayal, and ritual onto the landscape itself.

name: Andrzej Żuławski
teaser: Polish provocateur of the Possession generation — his films are shrieking, operatic collisions of love and madness that most censors couldn't stomach.

exploreAction.instruction: Don't try to understand it at first. Let the physical performance — the screaming, the writhing — register before the plot catches up.

name: Krzysztof Zanussi
teaser: Polish intellectual of the cinema — his films put scientists, priests, and rationalists in rooms together and watch them argue about how to live.

exploreAction.targetName: The Constant Factor (1980) — the first 25 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how Zanussi frames money and morality as a single problem. The mountain-climbing scenes are the movie's real argument.

name: Jean-Marie Straub
teaser: French-German director who, with partner Daniele Huillet, made austere adaptations of Brecht, Kafka, and ancient texts — cinema stripped to its bones.

exploreAction.targetName: Chronicle of Anna Magdalena Bach (1968) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Listen first: the film is built around music performed in full takes. Straub-Huillet treat cinema as a place where art gets its dignity back.

name: Guy Maddin
teaser: Canadian dreamer who makes silent-era melodramas out of found footage, wax, and Winnipeg snow — cinema as an invented memory of itself.

exploreAction.targetName: Brand Upon the Brain! (2006) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Let the exaggerated performances and tinted images wash over you. Maddin films autobiography the way silent films filmed nightmares.

name: Agnieszka Holland
teaser: Polish director who made personal films about resistance and moral gray zones, later landing in Hollywood without losing her edge.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how identity becomes a costume the hero keeps changing. Holland never lets you forget the price of each disguise.

name: Roy Andersson
teaser: Swedish director of absurdist tableaux — deadpan humans, pastel rooms, and the small catastrophes of ordinary life, each shot a painting.

exploreAction.targetName: Songs from the Second Floor (2000) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the fixed camera and the stage-like scenes. Andersson builds each shot like a diorama of human delusion.

name: Bille August
teaser: Danish director of sweeping period epics and quiet family dramas, twice awarded the Palme dOr for films about dignity under hardship.

exploreAction.targetName: Pelle the Conqueror (1987) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how a child and his father scrape by on a Danish farm. August films poverty with a warm, unblinking honesty.

name: Theodoros Angelopoulos
teaser: Greek master of the long take whose films drift across borders, history, and fog — time itself is the character he photographs.

exploreAction.targetName: Landscape in the Mist (1988) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Follow two children walking toward the border. Angelopoulos films their journey with the gravity of a national epic.

name: Dušan Makavejev
teaser: Serbian anarchist of cinema who collaged documentary footage, comedy, and explicit sex into political satire no one else dared attempt.

exploreAction.instruction: Expect a collage, not a story. Let the juxtapositions be the argument; Makavejev is editing ideas, not scenes.

name: Cristian Mungiu
teaser: Romanian New Wave anchor whose long, patient takes dissect daily life under compromised systems — a doctor's office becomes a moral arena.

exploreAction.targetName: 4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days (2007) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the camera refuses to look away from ordinary bureaucratic cruelty. Mungiu turns logistics into horror.

name: Cristi Puiu
teaser: Romanian director who set the New Wave's template: deadpan long takes, family tensions, and the unglamorous texture of real time.

exploreAction.targetName: The Death of Mr. Lazarescu (2005) — any 30-minute stretch
exploreAction.instruction: Follow one dying man through the night. Notice how many times a system can say no while staying entirely polite.

name: Radu Jude
teaser: Romanian provocateur who zigzags between satirical history lessons and essay films, always arguing with his country's past.

exploreAction.targetName: Bad Luck Banging or Loony Porn (2021) — the first 25 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Let the genre-hopping be the point: an essay, a street survey, a courtroom farce, all about who gets to judge.

name: Corneliu Porumboiu
teaser: Romanian minimalist whose comedies of bureaucracy — traffic cops, TV archives, housing blocks — find Kafka lurking in paperwork.

exploreAction.targetName: 12:08 East of Bucharest (2006) — end to end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch a town argue about whether its revolution happened on time. The camera barely moves; the comedy never stops.

name: István Szabó
teaser: Hungarian director who chronicled the twentieth century through compromised individuals — artists and doctors bending under history's weight.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the actor's face become the film's central moral instrument. Szabó builds a career's worth of compromise in one role.

name: Alexander Sokurov
teaser: Russian poet of the long take whose films move like paintings — he once shot an entire film in a single 96-minute Steadicam take.

exploreAction.instruction: Remember: one continuous take, no cuts. Let the museum's corridors become the film's argument about Russian history.

name: Kira Muratova
teaser: Ukrainian-born Soviet director whose absurdist, formally strange films were banned or shelved for years — and are now beloved cult objects.

exploreAction.instruction: Notice how the film jumps between two women's timelines. Muratova builds intimacy out of fragments and repetition.

name: Tengiz Abuladze
teaser: Georgian director whose allegorical trilogy on power and complicity became a touchstone of late-Soviet cinema.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the absurdist trial scenes with a straight face. Abuladze is asking who inherits guilt after a tyrant dies.

name: Otar Iosseliani
teaser: Georgian-born director of wordless, comic observations of everyday life, exiled from the USSR after criticizing its film bureaucracy.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the faces of the workers on the tea plantation. Iosseliani finds whole novels in a glance.

name: Sergei Parajanov
teaser: Armenian-born visual poet whose tableaux of folklore and faith are among the most image-dense films ever made. He painted with people.

exploreAction.targetName: The Color of Pomegranates (1969) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Forget plot. Read the film like a museum wall of living icons — each shot is a painting that moves a little.

name: Andrei Konchalovsky
teaser: Russian-born director who moved between Soviet epics, Hollywood, and intimate dramas, always chasing big themes through small lives.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how a Siberian village tracks a century of Russian history. Konchalovsky films the land as memory.

name: Ermanno Olmi
teaser: Italian humanist who filmed workers, farmers, and drifters with documentary patience, finding sacredness in ordinary labor.

exploreAction.targetName: The Tree of Wooden Clogs (1978) — the first 40 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how Olmi lets a full season pass without drama. Life's rhythm is the movie; the clogs are the symbol.

name: Maren Ade
teaser: German director of excruciatingly truthful social comedies — office hierarchies, family road trips, and the unbearable weight of expectations.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the awkwardness build in real time. Ade holds her scenes long enough for embarrassment to become love.

name: Matteo Garrone
teaser: Italian director who moves between Naples crime stories and dark fairy tales with the same anthropological eye for how people survive.

exploreAction.instruction: Notice what's missing: no heroes, no score, no glamour. The mafia is filmed like a factory's shift report.

name: Ciro Guerra
teaser: Colombian director who films the Amazon and the coast as characters — hypnotic voyages where myth and exploitation share a canoe.

exploreAction.targetName: Embrace of the Serpent (2015) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the black-and-white jungle double with a color version decades later. Guerra films colonialism as a river you travel twice.

name: Marco Bellocchio
teaser: Italian rebel of the 1960s who made explosive films about family, faith, and madness, still working six decades later.

exploreAction.targetName: Fists in the Pocket (1965) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how a family dinner becomes a chamber of psychological warfare. Bellocchio's debut never softens.

name: Ettore Scola
teaser: Italian director of bittersweet ensemble comedies that hid social history inside jokes — a restaurant table becomes a century of Italy.

exploreAction.targetName: We All Loved Each Other So Much (1974) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how three friends' lives interleave across decades. Scola cuts between their fates like a deck of cards.

name: Gillo Pontecorvo
teaser: Italian director of the anticolonial classic The Battle of Algiers, so real it was once used by the Pentagon for training.

exploreAction.targetName: The Battle of Algiers (1966) — the first 40 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch it like news footage — that's the point. Pontecorvo rebuilt a revolution with non-professionals and documentary grammar.

name: Francesco Rosi
teaser: Italian director who invented the investigative thriller — films that use the camera like a prosecutor building a case against the powerful.

exploreAction.instruction: Notice how the film starts with the death and works backwards. Rosi wants you to investigate, not just watch.

name: Liliana Cavani
teaser: Italian director of provocative philosophical films — The Night Porter asked whether victims and perpetrators can ever really separate.

exploreAction.targetName: The Night Porter (1974) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Hold the discomfort. Cavani is testing where complicity begins and whether memory can ever be escaped.

name: Maria Luisa Bemberg
teaser: Argentine director who came to film at fifty and made pointed period dramas about women trapped by the era they were born into.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch a forbidden love against a repressive state. Bemberg films defiance as a private, costly act.

name: Mario Monicelli
teaser: Italian master of commedia all'italiana who showed the poor laughing through misery — a comedian with a sociologist's eye.

exploreAction.targetName: Big Deal on Madonna Street (1958) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch a heist planned by people who can't even be trusted to hold a torch. Monicelli's genius is failing with style.

name: Luigi Comencini
teaser: Italian director of warm, precise films about children and the poor — often dismissed as gentle, often hiding real anger.

exploreAction.targetName: Bread, Love and Dreams (1953) — any 25-minute stretch
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how comedy and social observation share the same scenes. Comencini makes poverty funny without mocking it.

name: Arturo Ripstein
teaser: Mexican director of dark, still melodramas about family rot and desperation — Buñuel approved of him, which says almost everything.

exploreAction.targetName: Principio y Fin (1993) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how a family unravels in measured, gloomy steps. Ripstein films ruin the way others film romance.

name: Pablo Larraín
teaser: Chilean director who makes psychological portraits of public figures — Pinochet, Jackie Kennedy, Diana — as haunted interior dramas.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the film itself looks like a 1988 TV broadcast. Larraín uses the medium of advertising to end a dictatorship.

name: Sebastián Lelio
teaser: Chilean director of precise, empathetic portraits of women breaking free — from a Jehovah's Witness housewife to a trans rock star.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the dance floor scenes. Lelio lets a middle-aged woman be joyful, awkward, and alive without a single cruel joke.

name: Patricio Guzmán
teaser: Chilean documentarian who spent forty years filming his country's memory — first the coup, then the landscape that holds it.

exploreAction.targetName: Nostalgia for the Light (2010) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how astronomers and the mothers of the disappeared share the same desert. Guzmán films memory itself.

name: Miguel Littín
teaser: Chilean director who returned to Pinochet's Chile in disguise to make a secret film about his own country — a story Gabriel García Márquez wrote down.

exploreAction.targetName: Acta General de Chile (1986) — any 30-minute stretch
exploreAction.instruction: Watch it knowing the crew filmed under false identities. Every street scene is an act of resistance.

name: Ida Lupino
teaser: Actress turned director who in 1949 became one of Hollywoods only female filmmakers, tackling rape, polio, and bigamy in hard little noirs.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the only classic noir directed by a woman. Lupino strips the thriller to two men and a killer in a car.

name: Radu Mihăileanu
teaser: Romanian-French director of humane fables about refugees, train rides, and the stubborn refusal to give up hope at a border.

exploreAction.targetName: Train of Life (1998) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch a village stage its own deportation to survive. Mihăileanu makes tragedy swing like a comedy.

name: Isabel Coixet
teaser: Spanish director who shoots small, quiet stories about longing across languages and distances — often in English, often in winter light.

exploreAction.targetName: The Secret Life of Words (2005) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how two damaged strangers talk around their wounds. Coixet trusts silence more than speeches.

name: Icíar Bollaín
teaser: Spanish director of socially urgent dramas, from domestic abuse to the housing crisis, told through single, unforgettable protagonists.

exploreAction.targetName: Take My Eyes (2003) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the film shows love and control in the same gesture. Bollaín never lets you separate them.

name: Julio Medem
teaser: Basque director of ecstatic, spiral-shaped love stories that wind through landscapes, myths, and twin-like doublings.

exploreAction.targetName: Lovers of the Arctic Circle (1998) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the film spins in circles to tell its love story. Medem's camera moves like the plot does — around and around.

name: Alejandro Amenábar
teaser: Spanish director of elegant, twist-driven films — from a haunted orphanage to a paralyzed composer's inner world — who prizes feeling over gimmick.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how dread is built from fog, keys, and locked rooms. Amenábar scares you with manners, not monsters.

name: Nuri Bilge Ceylan
teaser: Turkish director of long, philosophical films about pride, loneliness, and marriage — landscapes shot like portraits and arguments that run for pages.

exploreAction.targetName: Once Upon a Time in Anatolia (2011) — the first 40 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the night driving scene. Ceylan turns a police search into a meditation on everything — time, memory, men.

name: Zeki Demirkubuz
teaser: Turkish director of spare, punishing films about fate, guilt, and Dostoevsky — he has adapted the Russian master more than once.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how stillness becomes menace. Demirkubuz holds shots long enough for the guilt inside them to surface.

name: Reha Erdem
teaser: Turkish director of dreamlike films where children, horses, and the sea stand in for everything adults won't say.

exploreAction.targetName: Times and Winds (2006) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how a village's seasons shape its children. Erdem films wanting with the patience of a weather report.

name: Semih Kaplanoğlu
teaser: Turkish director of the slow, luminous Yusuf trilogy — a boy, then a man, traced through seasons, faith, and memory.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the light on the wheat fields. Kaplanoğlu films waiting the way others film action.

name: Ferzan Özpetek
teaser: Turkish-Italian director of warm ensemble melodramas set in Rome and Istanbul, full of food, friendship, and secrets at the table.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the bathhouse becomes a character. Özpetek films steam, skin, and gossip like a slow tango.

name: Yavuz Turgul
teaser: Turkish screenwriter-director of crowd-pleasing epics about honor, migration, and the city — his gangster films carry real melancholy.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how a prisoner released after decades meets a country that forgot him. Turgul films the gap between promise and reality.

name: Lukas Moodysson
teaser: Swedish director who jumped from tender ensemble comedies about teens to the brutal poetry of Lilya 4-ever, then back to punk warmth.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how handheld intimacy turns into horror. Moodysson films a girl's fall with a camera that refuses to look away.

name: Ari Folman
teaser: Israeli director who animates memory itself — his Waltz with Bashir reconstructs a war from the dreams and gaps of the soldiers who fought it.

exploreAction.targetName: Waltz with Bashir (2008) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how animation lets memory hide and reveal. Folman draws the past because his characters cannot face it directly.

name: Annemarie Jacir
teaser: Palestinian director of understated road movies and family dramas that map displacement onto intimate, everyday life.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how a father and son deliver wedding invitations through the streets of Nazareth. Every doorstep is a small political essay.

name: Michel Khleifi
teaser: Palestinian-born Belgian director whose lyrical films set intimate family stories against the larger Palestinian memory.

exploreAction.targetName: Wedding in Galilee (1987) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how a wedding becomes a negotiation between occupier and occupied. Khleifi films tradition as quiet resistance.

name: Shadi Abdel Salam
teaser: Egyptian director of a single majestic masterpiece, The Mummy, which reimagined ancient Egypt in monumental, almost silent images.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the sand and the statues. Abdel Salam shoots antiquity with the gravity of a museum you can walk inside.

name: Mohamed Khan
teaser: Egyptian-Indian director who brought neorealist warmth to Cairo's streets, filming the city's poor with affection and humor.

exploreAction.targetName: The Wife of an Important Man (1988) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how Khan films Cairo like a neighbor, not a tourist. Small apartments, loud streets, real lives.

name: Khairy Beshara
teaser: Egyptian director of lively, politically sharp popular cinema who used thriller and melodrama forms to smuggle social critique.

exploreAction.targetName: Bitter Days, Sweet Nights (1988) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how genre and protest share the frame. Beshara makes a nightclub and a newsroom into political arenas.

name: Merzak Allouache
teaser: Algerian director who has spent four decades filming Algiers — first its youthful rebellions, later its everyday negotiations with the world.

exploreAction.targetName: Bab El-Oued City (1994) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how a neighborhood breathes as one character. Allouache films rooftops, stairwells, and loud arguments as civic life.

name: Nacer Khemir
teaser: Tunisian director and storyteller whose desert films are fairytales of calligraphy, wandering, and lost treasure.

exploreAction.targetName: Wanderers of the Desert (1984) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the dunes like paintings. Khemir turns a child's quest into a meditation on beauty and loss.

name: Moufida Tlatli
teaser: Tunisian director and editor whose films give women's inner lives the space cinema rarely allows them — memory, touch, and silence.

exploreAction.targetName: The Silences of the Palace (1994) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the servants' quarters and the palace mirror each other. Tlatli films the hidden labor behind elegance.

name: Raoul Peck
teaser: Haitian-born documentarian and fiction filmmaker who excavates colonial history — Lumumba, the Haitian revolution, James Baldwin — with forensic passion.

exploreAction.targetName: I Am Not Your Negro (2016) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to Baldwin's words over Peck's images. The film argues with the present using the past's own voice.

name: Sarah Maldoror
teaser: Guadeloupean-born pioneer of African cinema whose Sambizanga told the story of Angolan independence through a womans solitary walk.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the political and the domestic share one frame. Maldoror films revolution as it is lived at home.

name: Jean Rouch
teaser: French anthropologist-filmmaker who invented shared anthropology and let his West African collaborators improvise their own stories on camera.

exploreAction.targetName: Moi, un Noir (1958) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the men play themselves and invent their lives. Rouch turned documentary into collective fiction.

name: Marcel LHerbier
teaser: French silent-era modernist who filled his films with abstract sets and Expressionist light, a generation before the avant-garde got famous.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the machines and the money circulate like blood. LHerbier films capital with the fever of a silent epic.

name: Souleymane Cissé
teaser: Malian director whose blend of griot storytelling and modernist form produced African cinema's first Palme d'Or winner.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the light — it's the real protagonist. Cissé shoots a father-son myth in blinding sun and deep shadow.

name: Idrissa Ouédraogo
teaser: Burkinabé director of tender village dramas that showed African rural life with Neorealist warmth and earned Cannes glory.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the children's faces. Ouédraogo films friendship and prejudice in a village with a gentle, knowing hand.

name: Gaston Kaboré
teaser: Burkinabé director and film educator who built his country's cinema culture and told stories of children caught between worlds.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how silence carries the story of a mute boy. Kaboré films kindness and cruelty in equal, quiet measure.

name: Mahamat-Saleh Haroun
teaser: Chadian director who carries his country's cinema alone — spare dramas of refugees, fathers, and the desert roads between them.

exploreAction.targetName: A Screaming Man (2010) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how a pool cleaner's quiet life gets caught in a civil war. Haroun films the war's edge, not its center.

name: Med Hondo
teaser: Mauritanian-born revolutionary who directed searing satires of colonialism and dubbed Hollywood voices — including a famous king's roar.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch a ship built inside a warehouse become an empire. Hondo stages four centuries of exploitation in one set.

name: Jacques Demy
teaser: French director who painted everyday life in candy colors and had his lovers sing their feelings in full pop-musical form.

exploreAction.targetName: The Umbrellas of Cherbourg (1964) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how every word is sung — even small talk. Demy turns the simplest parting into an aria of regret.

name: Chris Marker
teaser: French essayist of the moving image who invented the photo-essay film and kept tinkering with memory, cats, and the future.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the one moving image in a film made almost entirely of stills. Marker builds a time-travel story out of photographs.

name: Louis Feuillade
teaser: French pioneer whose serial thrillers — an arch-criminal in black, an alluring thief in a catsuit — invented the crime saga on film.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch for the proto-superhero energy: masks, traps, chases. A century later, cinema still lives in this serial's shadow.

name: Abel Gance
teaser: French visionary of silent cinema who invented widescreen and triple-screen triptychs for his monumental Napoleon.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how three screens join into one image. Gance wanted cinema to feel like a symphony performed across walls.

name: Jean Epstein
teaser: French theorist-filmmaker who worshipped the close-up and believed cinema's essence was rhythm, texture, and the soul of things.

exploreAction.targetName: The Fall of the House of Usher (1928) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the fog and the faces. Epstein films Poe like a fever dream rendered in light.

name: Fernando Solanas
teaser: Argentine director whose fiery essays and road-movie tangos turned political cinema into poetry and got him banned from his own country.

exploreAction.targetName: The Hour of the Furnaces (1968) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Expect an essay, not a story. Solanas cuts between images, text, and testimony to build an argument you feel in your chest.

name: Jacques Becker
teaser: French director of elegant, humane films about prison, work, and love — he proved that precision and warmth can share a frame.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the digging scenes as pure cinema — no dialogue needed. Becker films craft with the suspense of a thriller.

name: Jean Grémillon
teaser: French director prized by cinephiles for films of great formal beauty — the sea, the salt marshes, and the people who work them.

exploreAction.targetName: The Lady of the Camellias (1934) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how Grémillon frames the sea against human longing. He films melodrama with documentary weather.

name: Jacques Rivette
teaser: French New Wave's secret master of the long, labyrinthine film — conspiracies, theater troupes, and running times that reach 13 hours.

exploreAction.targetName: Céline and Julie Go Boating (1974) — the first 40 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the game begin: two women, a strange house, and a story they keep re-entering. Rivette lets playfulness lead.

name: Bertrand Tavernier
teaser: French director and tireless cinephile whose films range from jazz-soaked noir to savage police corruption, always rooting for the underdog.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the music scenes as much as watch them. Tavernier films jazz the way it sounds — late, smoky, and alive.

name: André Téchiné
teaser: French director of delicate, weather-lit dramas about desire and family across generations — the South of France's emotional cartographer.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how four teenagers' friendships shift with the Algerian war news. Téchiné films adolescence as weather.

name: Olivier Assayas
teaser: French director who films the modern world's textures — global capital, artists, families — with restless, handheld intimacy.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how objects — a vase, a table — carry family memory. Assayas films inheritance as an argument with the past.

name: Leos Carax
teaser: French romantic of the New Extremity who makes operatic, self-destructive love stories — dancing, fire, and cinema itself as characters.

exploreAction.instruction: Let the film's rules stay unclear. Carax is less telling a story than conducting a ceremony about performance.

name: Patrice Leconte
teaser: French director of bittersweet romantic comedies and elegant thrillers, equally at home with mime, widows, and a lipstick-red murderess.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how wit becomes a weapon at court. Leconte makes verbal dueling feel like swordplay.

name: Cédric Klapisch
teaser: French director of ensemble comedies about young people in Paris, Barcelona, and shared apartments — life advice disguised as romcom.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how a shared apartment becomes a small Europe. Klapisch films youth as a loud, multilingual collage.

name: Mia Hansen-Løve
teaser: French director of quiet, radiant films about vocation and heartbreak — DJs, philosophers, young women becoming themselves.

exploreAction.targetName: Things to Come (2016) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how a philosopher's orderly life loosens. Hansen-Løve films change as a series of small, truthful mornings.

name: Justine Triet
teaser: French director of sharp, unruly dramas about women on trial — literally in Anatomy of a Fall, figuratively in everything she makes.

exploreAction.targetName: Anatomy of a Fall (2023) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how a marriage gets dissected in court. Triet turns every domestic detail into evidence.

name: Julia Ducournau
teaser: French body-horror radical whose films — cannibalistic coming-of-age, a driver turned living weapon — won Cannes and rewired the genre.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how appetite becomes the film's engine. Ducournau makes you feel the body as horror and as home.

name: Mathieu Kassovitz
teaser: French director whose La Haine turned the banlieue riot into a black-and-white epic that still defines French cinema's angry decade.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the long-take opening and the graffiti tag the trio keeps passing. Kassovitz films one night that never cools.

name: Jean-Jacques Beineix
teaser: French director of glossy 1980s cinema du look — neon, obsession, and the diva who sang for a dying boy.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opera-recording heist. Beineix turns a bootleg tape into the year's most stylish chase.

name: Claude Berri
teaser: French director and producer who made beloved adaptations of Pagnol's Provençal novels and bankrolled the New Wave's elders.

exploreAction.targetName: Jean de Florette (1986) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how a landscape's water becomes a family feud. Berri films greed with the patience of a farmer.

name: Bertrand Blier
teaser: French provocateur of odd-couple farce — he made Gerard Depardieu and Patrick Dewaere argue, charm, and outdo each other on screen.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch two drifters live by appetite alone. Blier's anarchic comedy hides real tenderness under the shocks.

name: Renato Castellani
teaser: Italian director of Romeo and Juliet on real Verona streets — a film so fresh it made Shakespeare feel improvised.

exploreAction.targetName: Romeo and Juliet (1954) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the non-professional teen leads against real Renaissance streets. Castellani films the play like a news story.

name: Carlo Lizzani
teaser: Italian director who traced his country's twentieth century — from wartime partisans to the Red Brigades — with a journalist's urgency.

exploreAction.targetName: The Violent Four (1968) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how a heist goes wrong in real time. Lizzani builds tension from procedure, not guns.

name: Valerio Zurlini
teaser: Italian director of melancholy youth films and searing war dramas whose visual elegance earned him a small, devoted cult.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how two brothers' love is told through memory fragments. Zurlini films loss with a painter's restraint.

name: Florestano Vancini
teaser: Italian director of The Long Night of 1943, a bleak small-town tragedy of fascism that ranks among Italy's harshest political films.

exploreAction.targetName: The Long Night of 1943 (1960) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how a town's silence enables atrocity. Vancini films complicity the way Hitchcock filmed suspense.

name: Vittorio De Seta
teaser: Italian documentarian who filmed Sicilian fishermen, miners, and shepherds in gorgeous color — real work, dignified and strange.

exploreAction.targetName: Lu Tempu di li Pisci Spata (1955) — end to end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch an eleven-minute film about swordfish hunting. De Seta makes labor look like ritual and ritual like labor.

name: Pietro Germi
teaser: Italian director who made savage Sicilian satires — the honor-code divorce farce Divorce Italian Style earned him worldwide fame.

exploreAction.targetName: Divorce Italian Style (1961) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how a man plans a murder as a social solution. Germi films the comedy of custom with a scalpel.

name: Alberto Lattuada
teaser: Italian director of neorealist tales and gothic comedies — he filmed Lombardy's poor and a bawdy Bell'Antonio with equal gusto.

exploreAction.targetName: The Mill on the Po (1949) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the river dominate the frame. Lattuada films a peasant revolt with the force of weather.

name: Maurice Pialat
teaser: French realist who filmed family cruelty and desire without mercy — a director who believed truth was more important than beauty.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the rawness of the performances. Pialat lets actors breathe and stumble like real people.

name: Claude Sautet
teaser: French director of quiet adult melodramas — men in bars, old friendships tested by new love — the poet of midlife melancholy.

exploreAction.targetName: The Things of Life (1970) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how a crash's aftermath unfolds in memory fragments. Sautet films a life reviewed at the moment it ends.

name: José Luis Garci
teaser: Spanish director of nostalgic, dialogue-rich dramas — his Begin the Beguine became Spain's first Oscar winner for best foreign film.

exploreAction.targetName: Begin the Beguine (1982) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the conversation scenes. Garci builds a whole post-war Spain out of what people say over drinks.

name: Sergio Corbucci
teaser: Italian maestro of the spaghetti western whose Django, a coffin and a machine gun, was darker and wilder than anything Leone dared.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the mud, the coffin, and the machine gun. Corbucci makes violence look like a bargain with the devil.

name: Grigori Chukhrai
teaser: Soviet director whose Ballad of a Soldier turned a war story into an aching human poem about one soldier's journey home.

exploreAction.targetName: Ballad of a Soldier (1959) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how a soldier's six days of leave become an epic. Chukhrai films war's cost in quiet, human gestures.

name: Marlen Khutsiev
teaser: Soviet director of I Am Twenty, a moody portrait of Moscow youth that captured the 1960s thaw better than any official film.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the city itself — streets, trams, parties — as the real character. Khutsiev films a generation drifting without a map.

name: Georgiy Daneliya
teaser: Soviet director of warm, wry comedies and the cosmic satire Kin-dza-dza!, beloved for finding tenderness in absurdity.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch a small-town pilot chase his dream to Moscow. Daneliya makes gentle comedy out of the gap between languages and lives.

name: Eldar Ryazanov
teaser: Soviet master of the romantic comedy whose New Year's classic The Irony of Fate is still broadcast every January 1 across Russia.

exploreAction.targetName: The Irony of Fate (1975) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how a drunk man ends up in the wrong city, in the wrong apartment, with the wrong woman. Ryazanov builds farce on Soviet urban uniformity.

name: Vladimir Menshov
teaser: Soviet director of Moscow Does Not Believe in Tears, the Oscar-winning saga of three women chasing love and careers across two decades.

exploreAction.targetName: Moscow Does Not Believe in Tears (1980) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the film jumps between 1958 and 1979. Menshov films a whole generation's bargains with fate.

name: Karen Shakhnazarov
teaser: Armenian-Russian director who mixed Soviet surrealism and satire — his Courier catches a teenager's rebellion against the system's boredom.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch a slacker who talks his way through a dead-end job. Shakhnazarov films youthful irony against a crumbling system.

name: Gleb Panfilov
teaser: Soviet director who made fierce films about women and power, built around his wife, the great actress Inna Churikova.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch a writer confront his own mediocrity in a provincial town. Panfilov films conscience as an argument with yourself.

name: Andrei Zvyagintsev
teaser: Russian director of austere, biblical-scale dramas about faith and corruption — Leviathan put a whole country on trial.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the landscape — sea, whale bones, gray sky — loom over the characters. Zvyagintsev films power as weather.

name: Pavel Lungin
teaser: Russian-French director whose Taxi Blues captured perestroika's chaos — a puritan saxophonist and a thuggish taxi driver forced together.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch two men who despise each other become roommates. Lungin films the Soviet collapse as a buddy comedy with bruises.

name: Yuli Raizman
teaser: Soviet director of The Communist, a portrait of the revolution's builders that both flattered and quietly mourned the system.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how one man's devotion outruns the machinery he serves. Raizman films idealism with a knowing sadness.

name: Sergei Bondarchuk
teaser: Soviet director and actor whose War and Peace remains the most expensive, most gigantic single film ever attempted — 600 extras per shot.

exploreAction.targetName: War and Peace (1966) — the battle of Borodino sequence
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the sheer scale — circling cameras, thousands of extras, and one woman's face in the middle of it all.

name: Aleksandr Ptushko
teaser: Soviet fantasy pioneer who filled the screen with giants, dragons, and magic — the Walt Disney of the East, if Disney were a bureaucrat.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the mid-century special effects with awe, not irony. Ptushko staged a whole myth with puppets, miniatures, and will.

name: Ivan Pyryev
teaser: Soviet director of operatic kolkhoz musicals — singing tractor drivers and dancing harvests — that Stalin loved and cinephiles still debate.

exploreAction.targetName: The Cossacks of the Kuban (1949) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the spectacle with fresh eyes: choreographed wheat, brass bands, and propaganda dressed as joy.

name: Yakov Protazanov
teaser: Russian pioneer who made Aelita, the 1924 science-fiction epic of a Martian civilization — Soviet cinema's first space trip.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the Constructivist Martian sets — triangles, geometry, and revolution in space. Protazanov made history look futuristic.

name: Aleksandr Dovzhenko
teaser: Ukrainian poet of Soviet cinema whose Earth turned the harvest into a luminous national elegy about death, grain, and renewal.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how a man's death and the wheat that grows after it become the same image. Dovzhenko films a whole world in faces and fruit.

name: Sergei Gerasimov
teaser: Soviet director and teacher who trained generations of Russian filmmakers and made the epic And Quiet Flows the Don.

exploreAction.targetName: And Quiet Flows the Don (1957) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the river and the steppe frame a family's tragedy. Gerasimov films Tolstoy's scope with a village's intimacy.

name: Mikhail Romm
teaser: Soviet director of Nine Days of One Year, the atomic-scientist drama that made physics look like the most romantic job on Earth.

exploreAction.targetName: Nine Days of One Year (1962) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch two physicists argue about safety, love, and progress over cigarettes. Romm films intellect as heroism.

name: Alexander Askoldov
teaser: Soviet director whose one film, Commissar, was banned for twenty years — a harrowing story of a Red Army woman and a Jewish family.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how a soldier's hardness cracks against a family's warmth. Askoldov films ideology meeting humanity head-on.

name: Vladimir Motyl
teaser: Soviet director of White Sun of the Desert, the beloved desert western cosmonauts watched before every launch.

exploreAction.targetName: White Sun of the Desert (1970) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch a Red Army soldier escort a harem across the desert. Motyl mixes action, humor, and folk-song melancholy into a genre all its own.

name: Leonid Gaidai
teaser: Soviet comedy genius whose slapstick masterpieces — Operation Y, The Diamond Arm — are quoted by every Russian speaker to this day.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch three comic shorts with vaudeville timing. Gaidai found comedy in queues, bureaucracy, and one very persistent trio of idiots.

name: Károly Makk
teaser: Hungarian director of Love, a two-woman chamber piece about memory and loyalty that slipped one of the era's most radical films past censors.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch a mother and daughter-in-law orbit a lie they both maintain. Makk films kindness as a form of resistance.

name: Márta Mészáros
teaser: Hungarian director of Adoption, the first Hungarian film by a woman, and a lifelong chronicler of mothers, daughters, and the gaps between them.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch two women from different generations talk honestly about children and choice. Mészáros films intimacy without decoration.

name: Ildikó Enyedi
teaser: Hungarian director of On Body and Soul, the dreamy Oscar-nominated romance between two colleagues who discover they share the same dreams.

exploreAction.targetName: On Body and Soul (2017) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the deer dream sequences. Enyedi films two loners finding each other in a place where words don't reach.

name: László Nemes
teaser: Hungarian director of Son of Saul, the Holocaust film that refuses to look away — shot in tight close-up with the horror always just out of frame.

exploreAction.targetName: Son of Saul (2015) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the shallow focus traps you with Saul. Nemes makes the off-screen space the source of dread.

name: Kornél Mundruczó
teaser: Hungarian director of volatile, confrontational dramas — his White God turned Budapest's stray dogs into an army of reckoning.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the dogs take over the city. Mundruczó films an uprising that is also a metaphor, and lets both be real.

name: Zoltán Fábri
teaser: Hungarian director of literary adaptations and stark war dramas, twice nominated for the Oscar for films about conscience and complicity.

exploreAction.targetName: The Fifth Seal (1976) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch five men argue about heroism in a shop at night. Fábri turns philosophy into a thriller about who will break first.

name: Péter Bacsó
teaser: Hungarian director of The Witness, a satirical masterpiece banned for twelve years — a fruit inspector who accidentally becomes a leader.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the absurdist rise of a small man in a big system. Bacsó's satire was so sharp the state shelved it for over a decade.

name: András Kovács
teaser: Hungarian director of Cold Days, the postwar reckoning film that asked a town to remember what its people did in the war.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch four men reconstruct a massacre from memory, each version shifting blame. Kovács films history as an argument without an ending.

name: György Fehér
teaser: Hungarian minimalist who, with filmmaker-composer Mihály Vig, made bleak, trance-like films of crime and punishment in grainy black and white.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the fixed, patient camera and the repeating music. Fehér turns a murder plot into a slow ritual of doom.

name: Gyula Gazdag
teaser: Hungarian director of inventive satires and later a beloved teacher of American indie filmmaking at UCLA.

exploreAction.targetName: The Whistling Cobblestone (1972) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch a young worker's absurd odyssey through bureaucracy. Gazdag films the system as a maze with no exit and lots of doors.

name: Ferenc Kósa
teaser: Hungarian director of The Upthrown Stone, a lyrical family saga spanning three generations of a Hungarian village.

exploreAction.targetName: The Upthrown Stone (1969) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how a family's history is told through a boy's eyes. Kósa films the land and the men who work it as one story.

name: Péter Gothár
teaser: Hungarian director of Time Stands Still, a generation portrait of teenagers coming of age inside the hushed late-1950s.

exploreAction.targetName: Time Stands Still (1982) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch a boarding school become a pressure cooker of secret songs and stolen radios. Gothár films adolescence as historical memory.

name: Gábor Bódy
teaser: Hungarian avant-garde theorist and filmmaker whose dense, encyclopedic films merged philosophy, video art, and cinema — he died at 39.

exploreAction.targetName: Narcissus and Psyche (1980) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Let the collage of film stocks and eras wash over you. Bódy was building a cinema of ideas, not stories.

name: Zsolt Kézdi-Kovács
teaser: Hungarian director of Forbidden Relations, a blunt rural drama about a sister and brother who fall in love and face a village's judgment.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the village reacts before the couple does. Kézdi-Kovács films taboo as a social, not private, event.

name: Ágnes Kocsis
teaser: Hungarian director of quiet observational dramas — her Fresh Air follows a teenage girl whose father returns to a home that moved on.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the everyday details — smoking, working, eating — that make up a girl's world. Kocsis films absence without melodrama.

name: Szabolcs Hajdu
teaser: Hungarian director of loose, ensemble family dramas — his Bibliothèque Pascal mixed social realism with Kafkaesque fantasy.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how a fairy tale and a trafficking story occupy the same film. Hajdu refuses to separate fantasy from cruelty.

name: Nimród Antal
teaser: Hungarian-American director who moved from Budapest crime thrillers to Hollywood survival horror — a genre craftsman with a feel for pressure.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch subway ticket inspectors hunt a mysterious pusher. Antal films a subterranean Budapest with deadpan style and real menace.

name: György Pálfi
teaser: Hungarian formalist of Taxidermia — a century-spanning triptych of gluttony, sex, and taxidermy told with baroque, absurdist invention.

exploreAction.instruction: Expect the grotesque to be beautiful. Pálfi films appetite as history — from a soldier's fantasy to a man who stuffs animals.

name: Benedek Fliegauf
teaser: Hungarian director of hypnotic, wordless dramas and the climate-myth allegory Womb — cinema as atmosphere first, story second.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how style replaces plot — long shots, loud music, a man drifting through a Budapest of low deals. Fliegauf films trance states.

name: István Gaál
teaser: Hungarian director of The Falcons, a spare, brooding fable of an aging falconer and a young rebel on the Hungarian plains.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the birds and the men who carry them. Gaál films a vanishing way of life with mournful precision.

name: Carl Theodor Dreyer
teaser: Danish director of The Passion of Joan of Arc, one of the most intense films ever made — faces, walls, and faith, nothing else.

exploreAction.targetName: The Passion of Joan of Arc (1928) — end to end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the close-ups — almost the entire film is faces. Dreyer films a soul under interrogation without cutting away.

name: Thomas Vinterberg
teaser: Danish co-founder of Dogme 95 whose Festen turned a birthday dinner into a family bomb, and whose Another Round made drinking a science.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the handheld camera and the unbroken dinner-table dread. Vinterberg films a family being dismantled one toast at a time.

name: Susanne Bier
teaser: Danish director of shattering family dramas — Open Hearts and In a Better World — who films grief as a contact sport.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how one car accident rearranges three lives. Bier films emotional damage with documentary immediacy.

name: Lone Scherfig
teaser: Danish director of warm, witty ensemble dramas — An Education and Italian for Beginners — who finds the comedy in awkward kindness.

exploreAction.targetName: Italian for Beginners (2000) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch six lonely people learn Italian together. Scherfig films a romance in the making with gentle, dry humor.

name: Tomas Alfredson
teaser: Swedish director of Let the Right One In, the vampire film told entirely from a bullied boy's winter — and the icy Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy.

exploreAction.targetName: Let the Right One In (2008) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the snow and the silence do the scaring. Alfredson films horror as loneliness, and loneliness as horror.

name: Jan Troell
teaser: Swedish director and cinematographer of the emigration epic The Emigrants — a painterly chronicle of Swedes crossing an ocean.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how Troell films the land before and after the crossing. The same soil means something different to the same people.

name: Bo Widerberg
teaser: Swedish director who fought the Bergman monopoly — his Elvira Madigan made a doomed love affair look like a summer painting.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the Mozart-soundtracked picnic scenes. Widerberg films happiness the way tragedy films it — in full, doomed color.

name: Vilgot Sjöman
teaser: Swedish provocateur of I Am Curious (Yellow), the banned, playful essay-film that merged politics, sex, and self-interview into one scandal.

exploreAction.targetName: I Am Curious (Yellow) (1967) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Expect a collage, not a plot. Sjöman films a country interviewing itself about class, love, and revolution.

name: Lasse Hallström
teaser: Swedish director of My Life as a Dog who went to Hollywood and made films about quiet, stubborn goodness — and a very famous dog.

exploreAction.targetName: My Life as a Dog (1985) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch a boy cope with loss through humor and imagination. Hallström films childhood's defenses with affection.

name: Joachim Trier
teaser: Norwegian director of melancholic city films — Oslo, August 31st and The Worst Person in the World — about smart people stuck in their heads.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch one day in the life of a man on leave from rehab. Trier films the city as a chorus of other people's lives.

name: Eskil Vogt
teaser: Norwegian screenwriter of Joachim Trier's films who directs his own quiet, unsettling studies of children and perception.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch children discover powers no adult can see. Vogt films growing up as a horror movie about empathy.

name: Bent Hamer
teaser: Norwegian director of deadpan, wry comedies — Eggs and Kitchen Stories — where small-town ritual becomes quietly hilarious.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch researchers observe bachelor farmers without being allowed to talk to them. Hamer films loneliness as a science experiment.

name: Nils Gaup
teaser: Sámi-Norwegian director of Pathfinder, the Oscar-nominated Arctic legend that put indigenous storytelling on the world screen.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the frozen landscape and the chase that defines it. Gaup films a myth with the urgency of a thriller.

name: Jörn Donner
teaser: Finnish-Swedish director, producer, and provocateur who financed and produced Ingmar Bergman's Fanny and Alexander and made films of his own.

exploreAction.targetName: Portraits of Women (1970) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch four women's monologues about their lives. Donner lets the camera simply sit and listen.

name: Mika Kaurismäki
teaser: Finnish director — the elder Kaurismäki — who makes warm, ragged road movies about musicians and drifters across Finland and beyond.

exploreAction.targetName: Helsinki Napoli All Night Long (1987) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch a Finnish taxi driver's surreal night. Kaurismäki mixes deadpan comedy with a traveler's restlessness.

name: Paul Verhoeven
teaser: Dutch provocateur who made shocking art — Turkish Delight, Elle, and the sci-fi satires RoboCop and Starship Troopers — in two languages.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the film refuses to make its heroine a victim. Verhoeven films violation, power, and gamesmanship with unnerving cool.

name: Charles Crichton
teaser: British Ealing comedy master of The Lavender Hill Mob and, forty years later, the surprise hit A Fish Called Wanda.

exploreAction.targetName: The Lavender Hill Mob (1951) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch a timid bank clerk plan the perfect bullion heist. Crichton turns crime into the politest mayhem ever filmed.

name: Alexander Mackendrick
teaser: British-American director of The Man in the White Suit and Sweet Smell of Success, the most cynical film ever made about publicity.

exploreAction.targetName: Sweet Smell of Success (1957) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the rat-a-tat dialogue and the night streets. Mackendrick films power the way a photographer films a bruise.

name: Carol Reed
teaser: British director of The Third Man, the Vienna noir whose zither score and sewer chase still define cinematic atmosphere.

exploreAction.targetName: The Third Man (1949) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the tilted angles and the shadows of post-war Vienna. Reed turns a city into a character with a secret.

name: David Attenborough
teaser: British broadcaster and director who practically invented the nature documentary, taking cameras where no one had filmed life before.

exploreAction.targetName: The Trials of Life (1990) — any one episode
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the sequence about parenting in the animal world. Attenborough treats behavior as story, and story as science.

name: Werner Schroeter
teaser: German queer cinema pioneer whose operatic, painted films about passion and madness inspired an entire generation, including Fassbinder.

exploreAction.targetName: The Death of Maria Malibran (1972) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Let the singing, the gestures, and the color carry you. Schroeter films opera as the truest form of feeling.

name: Ulrich Seidl
teaser: Austrian director of unflinching documentaries and dramas about bodies, belief, and boredom — filmed with a glare that never blinks.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch two parallel journeys — a Ukrainian nurse west, a Ukrainian orderly east. Seidl films Europe's labor traffic without comment.

name: Jessica Hausner
teaser: Austrian director of eerie, symmetrical films — Lourdes and Little Joe — where the uncanny hides inside clean, well-run places.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the wheelchair queue and the clinical lighting. Hausner films miracles as bureaucratic events.

name: Christian Petzold
teaser: German director of cool, precise dramas about identity and survival — Barbara, Phoenix — where history hides inside love stories.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch a survivor return to the man who may have betrayed her. Petzold films the present as a haunted house of the past.

name: Fatih Akin
teaser: German-Turkish director of Head-On and In the Far, films about love and belonging that burn across cultures and languages.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch two people crash into each other to escape their own lives. Akin films love as a wreck you choose.

name: Andreas Dresen
teaser: German director of Summer in Berlin and Cloud 9, whose handheld realism about ordinary people earned him a devoted following.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch a late-life affair filmed without judgment. Dresen treats the body's desires with matter-of-fact tenderness.

name: Margarethe von Trotta
teaser: German director of The Lost Honor of Katharina Blum and Marianne and Juliane — political films built around women's friendship and conscience.

exploreAction.targetName: Marianne and Juliane (1981) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch two sisters choose opposite sides of a revolution. Von Trotta films politics through the bond that survives it.

name: Wolfgang Petersen
teaser: German director of Das Boot, the claustrophobic U-boat epic, who crossed to Hollywood for Air Force One and The Perfect Storm.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the space — narrow, wet, and full of men. Petersen turns a submarine into the whole world.

name: Rolf Thiele
teaser: German director of the scandalous Rosemary, a fictionalized portrait of a high-class prostitute that pushed 1950s West German cinema's limits.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how glamour and corruption share the same dresses. Thiele films the Wirtschaftswunder's dark underbelly.

name: Jerzy Kawalerowicz
teaser: Polish director of Night Train and Mother Joan of the Angels — formally daring films that made silence and composition feel revolutionary.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch a sleeper car become a stage for strangers' secrets. Kawalerowicz films anxiety in confined, beautiful space.

name: Andrzej Munk
teaser: Polish director of Ashes and Diamonds' rival and The Passenger, whose unfinished masterpiece asked who gets to tell a war story.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch a loser's comic attempts to join every side of history. Munk films a man who is always one step behind the times.

name: Juliusz Machulski
teaser: Polish director of Vabank, the stylish 1980s heist comedy, and a string of popular genre films that smuggled satire past censors.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch a pianist plan revenge on the banker who ruined him. Machulski films a 1930s con with jazz and razor timing.

name: Krzysztof Kieślowski
teaser: Polish master of the moral weight of small choices — from documentary shorts to the Three Colors trilogy, he filmed fate as coincidence.

exploreAction.targetName: The Double Life of Véronique (1991) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the amber light and the mirroring lives. Kieślowski films the feeling of having almost met yourself.

name: Janusz Majewski
teaser: Polish director of elegant period dramas and the classic queer prison story Kings of Life, crafted with literary precision.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch a master tailor's orderly world shift. Majewski films craft as character — the work reveals the man.

name: Walerian Borowczyk
teaser: Polish animator and surrealist whose live-action films mixed medieval erotica, fairy tales, and avant-garde technique into a unique fever.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch a medieval castle romance filmed like a series of tapestries. Borowczyk's restraint makes the desire sharper.

name: Tadeusz Konwicki
teaser: Polish novelist-director of The Last Day of Summer and The Jump, whose haunted, foggy films made memory feel like weather.

exploreAction.targetName: The Last Day of Summer (1958) — end to end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch two strangers on an empty beach talk their way through a relationship in one day. Konwicki films the conversation as the whole plot.

name: Janusz Kijowski
teaser: Polish director of The Constant Factor's rival and the intimate State of Weightlessness, chronicling 1970s discontent through small lives.

exploreAction.targetName: State of Weightlessness (1980) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch a young man on the make inside a system that has stopped rewarding talent. Kijowski films ambition as drift.

name: Jiří Trnka
teaser: Czech puppet master who made A Midsummer Night's Dream and The Hand, the anti-censorship parable that got his studio closed.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch a potter's hand refuse to obey the state's giant hand. Trnka's puppet film is one of cinema's bravest acts of defiance.

name: Otakar Vávra
teaser: Czech director of the national epic Jan Hus trilogy and a career that spanned every regime — and was complicated by all of them.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the medieval spectacle and the sermon at its center. Vávra films faith as a political act.

name: Juraj Jakubisko
teaser: Slovak surrealist of the Czech New Wave whose baroque, folkloric fantasies — Birds, Orphans and Fools — were banned for years.

exploreAction.targetName: Birds, Orphans and Fools (1969) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch three orphans celebrate life in a bombed city. Jakubisko films joy and war in the same golden frame.

name: Elmar Klos
teaser: Czech director who, with Ján Kadár, made The Shop on Main Street, the Oscar-winning drama of complicity in occupied Slovakia.

exploreAction.targetName: The Shop on Main Street (1965) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch a man slide into a caretaker role he never wanted. Klos and Kadár film the moment responsibility arrives too late.

name: Pál Gábor
teaser: Hungarian director of the 1960s generation portrait Angi Vera, a political drama that measured a young woman's rise against her conscience.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch a promising young woman learn the system's true curriculum. Gábor films the price of getting ahead.

name: Ján Kadár
teaser: Slovak-Czech director of The Shop on Main Street, whose gentle humanism kept working through exile in the United States.

exploreAction.targetName: The Angel Levine (1970) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch a Jewish tailor and a Black angel argue about belief. Kadár films faith as a conversation, not a conversion.

name: Stevan Petrović
teaser: Serbian director of the WWII partisan thriller Seven, a stylized account of one man's escape that became a Yugoslav classic.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the countdown structure and the spare, violent set pieces. Petrović films escape as a stripped-down ritual.

name: Živojin Pavlović
teaser: Serbian director of When I Am Dead and Gone, a film that grounded the Yugoslav Black Wave in the raw lives of workers and drifters.

exploreAction.targetName: When I Am Dead and Gone (1967) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch a folk singer drift through Belgrade's margins. Pavlović films song, drink, and desperation with documentary gravity.

name: Michael Powell
teaser: Powell's Peeping Tom was so reviled on release that it ended his career — decades later it was re-examined as a masterpiece of British horror.

exploreAction.targetName: The Red Shoes (1948), the ballet sequence
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the 15-minute ballet — Powell cuts between reality and the stage world so seamlessly that you stop being able to tell them apart. That confusion is the point: art consumes the dancer.

name: Vittorio De Sica
teaser: De Sica cast a real unemployed man and his real son for Bicycle Thieves — they'd never acted before, and the film's authenticity rewrote world cinema.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the ending on the street — the father's breakdown in front of his son. De Sica refused to film it in a studio: the crowd is real, and their stares become the film's final verdict.

name: Victor Fleming
teaser: Fleming was the third director on Gone with the Wind — the first two were fired, and he took over mid-production, shooting the film's most famous scenes under impossible pressure.

exploreAction.targetName: Gone with the Wind (1939), the Atlanta fire sequence
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the burning of Atlanta — the fire was real, shot with a dozen cameras and hundreds of extras. Fleming staged the studio's biggest set ever and burned it to the ground in one take.

name: Frank Capra
teaser: Capra's It's a Wonderful Life flopped on release and only became a Christmas classic after the studio's copyright lapsed and TV stations played it for free.

exploreAction.targetName: It's a Wonderful Life (1946), the final 25 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the ending — George Bailey running through Bedford Falls, discovering he's 'the richest man in town.' Capra's most radical idea: the film's hero is a man who never left his hometown.

name: Howard Hawks
teaser: Hawks worked in every genre — westerns, comedies, noir, war — and said a good movie is 'three great scenes and no bad ones.' He made about 40 of them.

exploreAction.targetName: His Girl Friday (1940), the first 15 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the overlapping dialogue — Hawks had actors talk over each other, a novelty in 1940. The movie moves at the speed of a newsroom; notice how much plot arrives in the first ten minutes.

name: Michael Curtiz
teaser: Curtiz directed Casablanca while the studio was churning out war films — he treated it as just another assignment, and it became one of the most quoted movies ever made.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the refugees, the passport chase, the arrival of Rick. Curtiz establishes an entire world of desperation before his hero says a word. Notice how every character is introduced by their relationship to escape.

name: Elia Kazan
teaser: Kazan directed Streetcar and On the Waterfront, both with Marlon Brando, and trained most of the Method actors who defined 1950s Hollywood.

exploreAction.targetName: On the Waterfront (1954), the taxi scene
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the famous taxi confession — 'I coulda been a contender.' Kazan's camera stays on Brando's face; the scene is a masterclass in Method acting and the reason the film survives its own politics.

name: Nicholas Ray
teaser: Ray's Rebel Without a Cause gave teenage alienation its visual language — James Dean's red jacket and the knife fight are pure Ray.

exploreAction.targetName: Rebel Without a Cause (1955), the first 20 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — Jim Stark drunk in the street, the toy monkey, the family. Ray shot in WarnerColor and widescreen, making teenage angst look operatic. Notice the red jacket: Ray's color code.

name: Alain Resnais
teaser: Resnais's Hiroshima mon amour opened with documentary footage of the bombing, then dissolved into a love story — memory and history tangled in the same frame.

exploreAction.targetName: Hiroshima mon amour (1959), the first 15 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening lovers' exchange over documentary footage. Resnais refuses to show the bomb — only its aftermath, repeated like a memory loop. Notice how the voiceover argues with the images.

name: Pier Paolo Pasolini
teaser: Pasolini was a poet, novelist, and Marxist before he was a director — his Gospel According to St. Matthew cast a real bricklayer as Jesus.

exploreAction.targetName: The Gospel According to St. Matthew (1964), the first 25 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — Pasolini shot the gospel in real Italian villages with real faces. The camera is often hand-held and the faces are untrained; it reads like a documentary of a miracle.

name: Kenji Mizoguchi
teaser: Mizoguchi's films are almost all about women suffering under male power — his sister was sold into geisha service when he was a child, and he never stopped filming that wound.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the final shot — a long take of the widow at her husband's grave. Mizoguchi held his camera motionless for minutes at a time; the stillness becomes grief you can stand in.

name: Emir Kusturica
teaser: Kusturica's Underground won the Palme d'Or by telling Yugoslavia's collapse as a wild, drunken circus — his films move at the speed of a brass band falling downstairs.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the brass band, the tank, the wedding. Kusturica stages chaos as choreography. Notice how every scene is built on music and movement, not dialogue.

name: Takashi Miike
teaser: Miike has directed over a hundred films across every genre — including a children's film and the most notorious horror films ever made — often shooting several a year.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the first half — a gentle romance, then the bag, then the phone call. Miike's most famous trick is the tonal turn: notice the exact moment the film stops being kind.

name: Jia Zhangke
teaser: Jia films the places China's economic boom left behind — his movies are a documentary record of a country demolishing itself into the future.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — a state dance troupe in the 1980s practicing in a shabby hall. Jia tracks how clothes, music, and dance change as China changes. Notice the haircuts: that's the timeline.

name: Chantal Akerman
teaser: Akerman's Jeanne Dielman is a 3.5-hour film about a woman peeling potatoes and making beds — in 2022, Sight & Sound ranked it the greatest film ever made.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the first half hour — household chores in real time, shot head-on. Akerman's radical claim: domestic labor is worthy of cinema's full attention. Notice when the routine breaks.

name: Mel Brooks
teaser: Brooks was a comedy writer for Sid Caesar's Your Show of Shows before directing — he won an Oscar for his 11-minute short The Critic, then spent years convincing studios to let him make The Producers.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the musical number that nearly ended his career before it started. Brooks's joke is that bad taste, performed with total sincerity, becomes art. Notice the precision of the choreography inside the chaos.

name: Sydney Pollack
teaser: Pollack was also a character actor — he played the agent in Tootsie and Dustin Hoffman's boss in Eyes Wide Shut, and directed 20 features between his cameos.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — Michael Dorsey's agent (Pollack himself) trying to talk sense into him. The film's joke is that Pollack cast himself as the frustrated voice of reason.

name: Robert Zemeckis
teaser: Zemeckis met Steven Spielberg when Spielberg saw his student films at USC — Spielberg then produced the movie that made Zemeckis famous, Back to the Future.

exploreAction.targetName: Back to the Future (1985), the first 20 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the clocks, the Delorean, the Libyans. Zemeckis sets up the entire trilogy's rules in the first act: time travel, consequences, and a clock that's always running.

name: Robert Aldrich
teaser: Aldrich made The Dirty Dozen and Whatever Happened to Baby Jane? — he was a contract director who outlasted the studio system by being tougher than it.

exploreAction.targetName: Whatever Happened to Baby Jane? (1962), the first 20 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the child star, the accident, the sisters frozen in time. Aldrich stages the horror of aging inside one house; notice how the house itself becomes a prison.

name: Sam Peckinpah
teaser: Peckinpah's The Wild Bunch made slow-motion violence an art form — the studio thought he'd destroyed the film, and audiences made it a hit.

exploreAction.targetName: The Wild Bunch (1969), the opening shootout
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening massacre — children watching a gang's violence as if it were theater. Peckinpah's slow motion makes each death a choice. Notice the children's faces: the film's conscience.

name: William Friedkin
teaser: Friedkin got the directing job on The Exorcist partly because he'd made The French Connection — the studio wanted a realist to shoot the supernatural.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening in Iraq — the archaeology dig, the statue, the wind. Friedkin spends the first act in a completely different world, so the horror arrives slowly. Notice the sound design: the wind is a character.

name: George A. Romero
teaser: Romero invented the modern zombie with Night of the Living Dead — he was a commercial filmmaker who shot the film on weekends with borrowed money and cast his friends.

exploreAction.targetName: Night of the Living Dead (1968), the first 20 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the cemetery, the first zombie, the farmhouse. Romero made the film for $114,000 and it outgrossed many studio pictures. Notice the grainy black-and-white texture — that's poverty becoming style.

name: Tobe Hooper
teaser: Hooper's The Texas Chain Saw Massacre was rated X on release and banned in several countries — it's now in the National Film Registry for its influence on horror.

exploreAction.targetName: The Texas Chain Saw Massacre (1974), the first 20 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the radio news, the graveyard, the hitchhiker. Hooper shot in the Texas heat with a cast near collapse. Notice how the sun itself feels threatening — horror in daylight.

name: Wes Craven
teaser: Craven based Freddy Krueger's glove on a news story about a man who was attacked by a boiler worker — and Freddy's name came from a bully from Craven's childhood.

exploreAction.targetName: A Nightmare on Elm Street (1984), the first 20 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — Tina's dream, the boiler room, the glove scraping metal. Craven's idea was that the dream IS real. Notice how he breaks the rules of film grammar — the dream logic — to unsettle you.

name: Stanley Donen
teaser: Donen directed Singin' in the Rain with Gene Kelly — and choreographed most of the dance numbers himself before he was 30.

exploreAction.targetName: Singin' in the Rain (1952), the title number
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the rain dance and notice the tap tempo — Kelly's splashy joy is technically perfect, every step audible in the mix. Donen and Kelly built the number around a single puddle and a lamppost.

name: Vincente Minnelli
teaser: Minnelli directed some of MGM's greatest musicals — including Meet Me in St. Louis, starring his future wife Judy Garland — and his daughter is Liza Minnelli.

exploreAction.targetName: Meet Me in St. Louis (1944), 'Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas'
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the Christmas scene — Garland singing a song about separation to her screen sister. Minnelli stages the whole family's grief in one room. The song was written for the film and became a standard.

name: Gene Kelly
teaser: Kelly directed several musicals solo after learning the craft from Donen — he insisted on dancing in real locations, like the rain, because he thought dance belonged in the real world.

exploreAction.targetName: An American in Paris (1951), the final ballet
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the 17-minute dream ballet at the end. Kelly designed it as a living painting — every scene references a different French painter. Notice how the choreography becomes the plot's resolution.

name: Bob Fosse
teaser: Fosse directed All That Jazz, a movie about his own heart attack — he survived open-heart surgery in real life and turned it into a musical.

exploreAction.targetName: All That Jazz (1979), the opening 'audition' sequence
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the dancer's audition with the casting table, the heartbeat sound, the mirrors. Fosse's editing is staccato, like jazz. Notice how the film is already a confession.

name: Roger Corman
teaser: Corman produced over 400 films on tiny budgets and gave debuts to Coppola, Scorsese, Bogdanovich, and many more — his movies were shot in days, not weeks.

exploreAction.targetName: The Little Shop of Horrors (1960), the first 20 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the flower shop, the plant, the blood. Corman shot the film in two days by reusing the same sets. Notice how poverty of resources forces inventive camera angles.

name: Russ Meyer
teaser: Meyer's Faster, Pussycat! Kill! Kill! was a drive-in sensation — his films were cheap, fast, and so stylish that even the art world eventually embraced them.

exploreAction.targetName: Faster, Pussycat! Kill! Kill! (1965), the first 20 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the go-go dancers, the desert, the violence. Meyer shoots with a comic book's energy: wide angles, rapid cuts, and dialogue that's pure pulp poetry.

name: Hal Ashby
teaser: Ashby edited 2001 for Kubrick before directing — his films like Harold and Maude and Being There have a gentle, humane eccentricity that made him a 1970s icon.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — Chance the gardener watching television, his whole world. Ashby's joke is that the simple man's platitudes are mistaken for wisdom. Notice how the TV is framed like a window.

name: Terry Gilliam
teaser: Gilliam was the only American in Monty Python — he did the animated sequences — and his solo films like Brazil and 12 Monkeys mix comedy with dystopia.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the bureaucratic dream world, the giant ducts, the paperwork. Gilliam built a dystopia from office supplies. Notice how the sets look hand-built, like his animations come to life.

name: Gaspar Noé
teaser: Noé's Irreversible is famous for its backwards narrative and a nine-minute unbroken shot of violence — audiences walked out, and it's still discussed today.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening backwards scenes — the film runs in reverse, so you meet the ending first. Noé's camera spins and floats; notice how the chaos is choreographed. This film is an endurance test by design.

name: Franco Zeffirelli
teaser: Zeffirelli directed the 1968 Romeo and Juliet with real teenagers — Leonard Whiting was 16 and Olivia Hussey 15, and their casting changed how the play was performed forever.

exploreAction.targetName: Romeo and Juliet (1968), the balcony scene
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the balcony scene — Zeffirelli shot it in a real Italian courtyard with real light. His casting of actual adolescents made the romance feel dangerous and new. Notice the costumes: Renaissance, not Elizabethan.

name: Luchino Visconti
